en: The Compendium of the Glorious Densely Arrayed Conduct;
Chapter One: Homage to the Buddha.
Having prostrated to him who has reached the further shore of the ocean of all afflictions and the knowable,
the conduct of novice monks shall be compiled.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Homage to the Buddha," in the *Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha* compiled by Saṃghasena.
The second chapter:
The state of a novice;
he went for refuge with devotion to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Having undertaken the five precepts, he followed the Victor into homelessness.
For as long as life lasts, he abstains from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and false speech,
as well as from drinking intoxicants and from high and large beds or seats.

From dancing and the like, from perfumes, garlands, and so forth, from eating at improper times, and likewise from the acceptance of gold and silver—for these [transgressions], he is considered a *śrāmaṇera* by the Sage. (Śghs 2.3)
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The State of a Śrāmaṇera," in the *Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha* compiled by Saṃghasena.
The Third Chapter: The Means for Becoming a Śrāmaṇera.
1. The Training Rule on Abstinence from Taking Life.
The relinquishing of the vow occurs by means of the entire body or by a specific part of the body;
[the ascetic] shall not kill a living being, even one as small as a five-fingered insect.
One should not speak of the color of death, nor should one seek out a weapon-bearer;
one should not, with a murderous intent, employ anyone for the purpose of killing.
One should not perform purgation, emesis, ointments, the preparation of poisons, or the use of weapons for the purpose of killing living beings, nor should one cause the destruction of a fetus.
One who observes the vow should not take omens from dreams, the hooting of owls, and the like;
nor should one engage in misconduct,
even for the sake of attaining the fruits of generosity and ethical discipline.
The All-Knowing One has declared that when the mind is intent on killing— whether directed toward the middle, the rear, or the front— it is only the person being killed whom it harms, and no other.
One may employ the construction of magical devices such as artificial heads, pillars, or vetālas for the purpose of subduing or paralyzing [an enemy],
but one must not perform them for the sake of killing embodied beings.
On whatever path there may be danger from thieves, armies, and the like, the ascetic should not point out that road for the destruction of embodied beings. (Śghs 3.1.7)
And at that sacred ford where there may be danger from whirlpools caused by serpents—
for the purpose of crossing the river— one should not reveal that ford.
"Do not give even a small boon to the king; abandon your life!"—a mendicant should not speak such improper words when thus addressed.
Whatever fear may arise from snakes, [venomous] beasts, or yakṣas while dwelling there, one should not designate that [place] for a guest with the intention of killing him. Śghs 3.1.10.
If a deceitful person kills an enemy under the pretext that he is a tiger or the like,
he should be quickly expelled from the monastery by the monks.
One should act in such a way that not even a single person perishes;
one must not perform an unrighteous deed, remembering it to be like a saw.
And as for the novices who have been designated for execution and are about to be killed,
they should be expelled from the monastery simultaneously with the application of that [intention].
The assault, the perception of a human, the murderous intention,
and the destruction of life— these are the five factors in the killing of a human being.
If a novice monk (śrāmaṇera) performs acts such as administering poison or using weapons with the intent to kill,
and the person dies because of that very act, he would then become one who lacks restraint (asaṃvarin).

Indeed, one who kills a human being through ignorance—such as by killing a slave or similar persons—and who is not insane or otherwise deranged, incurs the loss of his vows [if he is a renunciant]. (Śghs 3.1.16)
A practitioner should always perform deeds of bodily loving-kindness and so forth toward sentient beings;
for it has been said by the compassionate ones: "Therefore, one should not harm sentient beings. (Śghs 3.1.17)
One should not afflict living beings with wooden stocks, ropes, or leather bonds; nor should one compel them to enter water or fire, or to undergo execution and the like.
Since the cultivation [of land] involves killing worms, oxen, and the like, as well as wrong livelihood, one should abandon it from afar. (Śghs 3.1.19)
One should not brand the noses of cattle, buffaloes, and the like, nor should one pierce their nostrils;
and a mendicant should not strike various living beings with canes or other such implements.
When a mendicant eats meat or a meat-based condiment prepared specifically for him, his mind becomes merciless; therefore, he should not eat it at all.

The object of knowledge, however, is examined through three modes: what is seen, what is heard, and what is suspected. That which is "seen" is what has been personally observed; that which is "heard" is what has been reported by a trustworthy person. (Śghs 3.1.22)
Because one sees the horns, wings, and so forth of deer and other animals bound in houses, the suspicion arises therein: "Was this killed specifically for my sake, or not? (Śghs 3.1.23)
If questioned, the donor should say: "These were killed for your sake. One who has desisted from the killing of living beings should not eat in that house.

Those killed by hawks and other predators [are not at fault], for they were consumed as rice, barley, and mung beans; there is no sin for those who eat them for the sake of their parents or for the sake of a sacrifice. (Śghs 3.1.25)
If meat, fish, or the like is prepared specifically for one wealthy person,
it is not permissible for other novices to consume it.
Knowing that water from rivers and other sources contains living beings, one should not drink it;
by "living beings" are meant even the most subtle creatures, such as those that tremble, move with ripples, or float about.
Indeed, a water-pot with its lid and carrying-net should be kept under control;
a sheath should be used at least for a well-washed garment in order to avoid damage.
For one who possesses divine vision or is blind, the inspection of water is not required;
however, for one who can see the whorls at the tips of their thumbs, it is not prohibited.
Lest there be a confusion of the eyes, one should not look at it for long;
indeed, one should not act with deceit or guile even for a single moment.
O lotus-eyed one, that interval of time during which an elephant sixty years old circles around a cart filled with bamboo is [the duration of a finger-snap]. Śghs_3,1.31.
There are three levels of ground even within the water—upper, lower, and middle;
whichever ground attains purity, by that [ground] the ascetic should perform his task.
If large insects go to the bottom when struck by the palm of the hand, that water should be strained with a five-fingered filter; otherwise, it should not be used.
In whatever water living beings might become stuck if their hands were immersed,
there a mendicant should not wash his hands, feet, face, or clothing.

When one has gone to a family, one should ask whether water has been poured out or not. If they say "no," one should say, "It is for the sake of the deceased"; otherwise, one should not say, "Pour it out."
But he who, having poured the water containing living organisms into his own vessel,
releases that which was brought back right there himself— [Śghs 3.1.36].
Alternatively, where water remains for seven days, one should place it in a monastery or in a vessel such as a cauldron; thus it will not dry up.
Or, when it has rained and the lord of rivers flows with a clear torrent of water,
one should dismiss [the deceased] with the words, "Go to the fall of the lord of rivers."
A traveler on the road should release water from below using a small vessel bound by two ropes with very long loops at their ends, while remaining in the water.
Having observed three ghaṭikās from a well while traveling on the road, if the water is pure, it may be drunk; otherwise, it must be strained.
Taking water from a rope-dipper when it contains living beings is not praised;
a mendicant must never be able to say "drink" or give [water] under such conditions.
One should not speak loudly to others regarding a pond or similar place containing living creatures;
when asked, one should reply to others, "Perform your task after careful consideration."
Regarding a pond or similar body of water, one should ask the preceptor whether it contains living beings or not; a mendicant must never practice deceit.
One must not water trees with impure water,
and likewise, one must not perform the bathing of preceptors and others with such water.

A renunciant should not drink head-washings, sour gruel, the supernatant of fermented barley, water struck by a staff, and so forth; nor should he give these to another, nor should he discard them on the ground.
One should not dry a bed infested with bugs in the sun;
nor should one cast it into snow, mud, or water that is cold or hot.
One should perform the rite for new construction with water containing living organisms;
having let it flow until the end of the day, that triangular mortar should be kept.
One should instruct the apprentice thus: "Bind the triangle;
lift up the lid and let the liquid flow out, and release the mortar."
Having caused that water to flow out by means of a seven-triangular ladle, one should then act against it;
having abandoned the task, one should go to another region.
These arise having not previously existed, and having existed, they pass into another state of being;
therefore, one who acts according to the prescribed rules should perform new karma.

One should avoid a bedstead or similar furniture that is draped with a fine cloth, as well as water in a river or other body of water that is less than four finger-breadths deep; these are prohibitions regarding new construction work.
The ascetic should carry a double-staff bound by a cord attached to two ear-holes,
as well as a water-strainer, outside of the alms-bowl.
With a mind overcome by compassion, one who perceives even salt water as pure should not discharge sweet water containing living beings into it without cause.

2. The training precept of abstaining from taking what is not given; the relinquishing of restraint; that which is for a limited time [or for a watch of the night]; that which lasts as long as life; and ghee and so forth.
An amulet bracelet that is not to be worn, whether it be deemed fit, unfit, or unallowable.
A mendicant should not take even the slightest thing belonging to another from the earth, water, bipeds, quadrupeds, those without feet, or trees. Śghs 3.2.2.
A mendicant who, with a thieving mind, takes wealth worth a quarter of a kārṣāpaṇa or even half of that, should be lightly expelled by others.
When an elephant has been led out from the enclosure on its four feet,
and when it has emerged from the closed gate, there should indeed be a pause (yati) at the point where the elephant is being led away.
When the stalk of the eye was bound at the ankle and pulled far from the surface of the earth,
the bird was like an elephant torn from its cage upon the breaking of its enclosure.
For he who leads away from his country or transfers wealth from his domain with a thieving mind incurs the downfall of violating the vows.
Having learned from a traveler that someone has died, a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) who,
while staying at the boundary, gives [the food] away and takes it up again, would be a non-ascetic ascetic.
The Sage declared that whatever wealth belongs to a deceased novice monk who has attained parinirvāṇa goes to his preceptor.
If the one observing the vow should take an elephant, he should go in the direction desired by the thief;
for that thief is the one observing the vow, while the elephant is designated as the "stolen" object.
Indeed, by releasing the two ends of the garland of robes used for worship,
when they fall to the ground, the ascetic falls away from his vow.
Having taken pearl necklaces and other such items cast away from that noble family, [he gave them].
Having placed it in a needle-case and having it carried by an attendant.
Or else, my child, was he taken by Jaṭālin because he had fallen from his vow? For is there a transgression of formal conduct merely by stepping off one's feet? Śghs_3,2.12 //
If someone binds cows, carts, horses, and so forth at night, and a mendicant [thinks], "They will carry these away," would he then be one whose vow has fallen? Śghs 3.2.13.
When a peg is straight, fixed, and firm, one who removes the necklace [therefrom] would be a thief; but not so when it is crooked or loose. (Śghs 3.2.14)
Just as one who pierces a jar and carries away its ghee, honey, oil, or water brings about the ruin of the city,
so too does a mendicant who causes a breach in his restraint incur a disturbance of his vows.
If, while a house is being partitioned between two brothers, a mendicant should desire a portion from one of them and take even a mere fragment of land,
his vow of restraint is broken.
If one who has lost hope recovers bowls or other items taken by thieves, he falls away from his restraint; however, one who is already fallen does not incur further transgression.
If something has been obtained through friendship, or given by cowherds and others,
then it is held that there is no offense for the ascetic who takes it.
One should display fear for the sake of obtaining a bowl and robes;
one should not go to the king and say, "We have been robbed by these thieves. Śghs 3.2.19.
If one says "I am taking that which belongs to the preceptors and teachers" while stealing what is their property,
both of them shall be thieves.
These two ascetics who steal their own property with a thieving mind shall be punished:
one shall be expelled after paying half the value, and the other after paying half a *niṣka*.
"We will serve you; stay at the gate and we shall commit the theft.
Having spoken thus, if one acts accordingly, there is an offense together with the thieves and novices.
When a guest monk has stayed and departed, if another monk comes later and, having forgotten his bowl and robes,
takes them and conceals them, he is indeed a thief.
In this way, all those residing there would have their vows impaired;
however, if that very person, having remembered [the transgression], brings it forth here, he is not indeed a sinner.
If a mendicant, with a thieving mind, causes another person to bring him a bowl,
he, as a practitioner of vows, thereby becomes guilty of an offense.
"As long as the worship of the Sage continues, so too does that of the Saṅgha;
he who gives [an offering] to another [instead] becomes one whose vow is impaired."
Having written it down, the withdrawal should be accepted from one another, from a stūpa, or from the Saṃgha;
and at the undertaking of the formal act (karman), it must be stated thus: "It is not otherwise for one who has not performed what was prescribed."
Having placed one's trust in the thought, "I shall give [it]" to those two— the thief and the one liberated from his own portion— between them, one does not meet with calamity.
"Whatever gain you obtain, I shall obtain that same gain;
thus, when a gain has arisen, the thief took half of it. (Śghs 3.29)
The same applies to the solicitation of alms; likewise for two who wear robes made of rags from dust-heaps:
whoever breaks the formal agreement (kriyākāra) thereby loses his restraint.
And food, drink, and so forth belonging to the Saṅgha should be given respectively to those who help and those who harm, as well as to the owners of the monastery, kings, and thieves.

The morning meal and other provisions belonging to the Saṅgha should be given even to those who are wealthy, provided they perform tasks such as plastering in the monastery; otherwise, it shall not be so.
Having given [the gift] to one who dwells on the boundary and serves as an attendant to the monks,
one may take rice and other provisions under the pretext of a child's meal-portion.
For one who has not yet abandoned hope may take back his lost bowl or robe;
thinking thus, a mendicant should never abandon hope regarding a lost bowl or other such items.
Those who, having undertaken the study and recitation of the scriptures, do not observe the communal discipline and the formal agreement, transgress what has been taught by the Jina.
A mendicant should certainly not take a banner as a sign from a stūpa;
rather, he may take a long strip of cloth that has been blown down by the wind.
A renunciant should not carry away another's property that is subject to toll, nor should he cause it to be carried;
he should not instruct others on the means for evading the payment of tolls.
If a merchant, having previously given a jewel to ascetics, later seeks it back,
saying, "You are deceiving me," that [jewel] should be returned after he has been thus rebuked.
There is no toll for a sage, nor for those observing vows regarding their personal requisites;
one who engages in buying and selling should pay a toll in regard to other goods.
The gain from the rainy-season residence should indeed be given to one who has completed the rains,
as well as to those two whose life or celibacy has come to an end.
The request for the rainy-season residence (varṣāvāsa) should be made by those who have arrived earlier and earlier;
by those who have arrived later, it should be made later, or simultaneously with the rest of the Saṃgha.
The All-Knowing One has also said this regarding one who, out of aversion toward the actual practice, abandons the state of a monk and undergoes initiation once again: Śghs_3,2.42.
Those who have not spent the rains retreat, those who are distracted, those with wrong views, the dead, and likewise those who have gone to another region— these five persons do not deserve a gain.
When a gain has arisen and the monk for whom it was intended has died, it must certainly be given to that specific designated monk. Śghs 3.2.44.
Even if he has gone to another country, one should place [the offerings] in the temple of Kalpa;
for the wise should certainly not give to those three who cause harm.
Thinking, "I shall give a cloak, a robe, or its price," one acquires [the gift] from those present through four formal steps; the gain is not obtained from others.
The gain of the rainy-season residence belongs to one who has completed the rains;
otherwise, there is no fault for another who does not accept it, provided it is according to the donor's wish.
The *kālika*, the *yāmika*, the *yāvajjīvika*, the *sāptāhika*, the *mṛta*, the *kṣudrapariṣkāra*, the *naityaka*, and the *akālacīvara*.
Through the realization of the consecration of the hut, birth, and so forth, there arises a great emergence;
one attains a tenfold gain from persons who have appeared before one.
A heavy object belonging to the Saṅgha, such as bedding or seating, must not be sold, nor should it be consumed; having made it one's own private property, it must not be used.
When a monk has given various articles to the Saṃgha of the four quarters that is present before him, he should offer them here and there accordingly.
When the Buddha has departed after giving silently, one should offer pearls and the like;
when he has turned his face toward the four directions, one should offer bedding, seats, and fine garments.
If one perceives a substantial object as belonging to another, possesses the intention to steal it,
and there is the removal from its place— when these five factors are present, one becomes a non-recluse (ayati).

Furthermore, another who possesses the perception that what he has given away belongs to himself and what he has acquired belongs to others does not lose his restraint merely by taking back a portion for the time being. Śghs 3.2.54.
Having taken what was not given, having leaped up and gone through the four directions in the sky, he sits down again in that very place; such a person has broken his vows.

Indeed, a mendicant who, out of ignorance, takes the property of another—whether it be something purchased or otherwise—incurs a violation of his vows, provided he is not insane or in a similar state. (Śghs 3.2.56)

3. The training precept of abstaining from sexual intercourse; the relinquishing of the vow consists of [engaging in] the male, female, or hermaphrodite [orifices], or the orifices of excrement, urine, or the mouth, using the generative organ.
Having cast it away, he should experience its taste; such a practitioner has violated his vow.
Humans, non-humans, animals, and beings such as men—
whether dead, asleep, or awake— should be known to be based upon sexual union.
Starting from an elephant down to the species of chickens,
whether small or large, the ascetic who approaches them falls away from his vow.
Being impassioned, one should not look at women nor listen to their voices; being naked, one should not approach the organ of generation nor indulge in it. Śghs 3.3.4.
Having joined together a hollow space (*koṭarī*) made between two walls—whether dry or damp—one should destroy it by means of a conflict; this applies when there is a gathering, and not otherwise.
Furthermore, one should not go toward a body that is divided into three parts, nor one that is bluish-black and bloated,
nor a skeleton, nor one smeared with blood and other fluids.
A mendicant who is always abstinent from sexual intercourse should not go near a woman, whether she be a skeleton of white bones, or one made of stone, wood, or cloth.
Having taken hold of one who is intoxicated by meditation and sloth, overcome by sleep,
distracted, or overwhelmed by painful sensations, he sits down firmly.
Having emerged from meditation, one should taste [the food] at the beginning, middle, and end;
it should be touched [with the tongue] while in the vihāra, but in the absence of tasting, it need not be done.
It is like the enjoyment of rice endowed with various seasonings and flavors;
and its tasting is like drinking oil, clear liquor, or fermented spirits.
The lack of relish for youth’s neck [of life] should be understood as being like a dog tied to a post of nectar, or like the touch of glowing iron for one who is delicate. Śghs 3.3.11.
Because of ignorance regarding what has been purchased and so forth,
the ascetic does not incur a transgression, provided he is neither insane nor mentally deranged.
One should not touch the aroused member for the sake of emitting semen, whether through contact with non-human beings or by means of the elements such as earth and so forth. Śghs 3.3.13.
If, through contact with an animal while intoxicated, semen should be emitted, the ascetic should reproach his own mind, thinking: "A loathsome deed has indeed been committed by me."
If seminal discharge occurs during dreams for a practitioner, there is not even the slightest fault in that emission of semen during sleep. (Śghs 3.3.15)
With a mind possessed by passion, Śrīghana should not touch a woman;
nor should he touch anyone else of such a kind, nor even a male or a neuter.
A monk who is impassioned should neither disparage nor praise the breasts, armpits, lips, navel, thighs, flanks, and hips of women. Śghs 3.3.17.
Whatever a woman might wish to do, in whatever manner she desires it,
one who is possessed of splendor should speak those very things accordingly in the presence of that woman.
She is the most excellent of women who would attend upon me in secret;
she shall obtain long life and other blessings, be free from disease, and possess great renown.
One whose mind is scorched by the fire of passion should not speak such words before women, nor likewise before men or eunuchs. (Śghs 3.3.20)
A novice monk should not act as a messenger for marriages or invitations;
nor should he even make gestures that constitute such a message.
"I would cause this faithful woman to give this girl to him"—such a statement does not fit with the *Arthasaṃsyandana-sūtra*. Śghs_3,3.22.
One who observes the vow should not give cows or other such things for the sake of seeds;
nor should he ever request these very things from others.
"Among these [women] you are equal; do not dwell even with a single woman"—thus indeed should an ascetic not speak to a man who has many wives.

If one says, "I possess the knowledge and vision of a Pratyekabuddha, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, or their disciples," while abstaining from false speech as a training rule, he is to be expelled for lying, except in the case of overweening pride.
He is not capable of accepting the knowledge of the dharma, subsequent knowledge, and so forth, nor perfect awakening to the truths, the five superknowledges, or vision. Śghs_3,4.2 //
Whether through the speech of noble ones or barbarians, or by means of writing, the hand-gesture,
or the claim of possessing knowledge and so forth— even that which is to be understood must be known as false.
I dwell alone at the foot of a tree; I find delight there, not in a house. My mind is concentrated, yet it is beyond the reach of words and the senses.
One should never speak in praise of oneself before the Buddhas and others;
when asked about another's virtue, one should speak of it in that person's presence, and not otherwise.
Whatever has been seen, heard, thought, or even known, that one should speak;
speaking otherwise than this, one is a speaker of falsehood. (Śrīghana) 3.4.6
When one perceives a real object as unreal, and likewise directs the mind accordingly,
speaking words with a false perception, one is a liar possessing five factors.
"He who speaks falsely here regarding [the number of syllables] joined with four, three, two, or one [syllable per line],
he should be known as a liar among other ascetics," so says Śrīghana.
A practitioner should not confront [an opponent] with what is untrue and groundless—such as [accusations of] killing living beings—with the intent to destroy or cause them to fall away. Śghs 3.4.9.
On account of even a minor offense, or by that which is merely a slight fault,
a novice monk (śrāmaṇera) should not openly revile others in the presence of the venerable ones (śrīghana).

A practitioner of vows should never, for the sake of making one who is crooked or lacking in eloquence feel inferior, incite them by means of talk regarding caste, gender, or actions, whether those be low, middling, or high.

For a practitioner observing the vows should never, under any circumstances, address a fellow ascetic with secondary afflictions, disease, abuse, transgressions, or the like, provided he maintains the intention previously described.
"He will fall into division and will seek reconciliation with another;
therefore, an ascetic should not practice slander by speaking of caste and the like."
5. The training rule regarding abstinence from drinking *surā*, *maireya*, and intoxicants:
since *madya*, *surā*, and *maireya* are the locus of negligence, they should not be given to another, nor should they be drunk, being like dog urine. (Śghs 3.5.1)
Some [liquor] is prepared from tree bark mixed with molasses, while another is made from bark alone; liquor is also produced from these: flour, fermenting agents, and water.
Indeed, that which is prepared from molasses, *dhātrī*, water, and *dhātakī*— known as *maireya*—
is not permitted even for ascetics to drink, even if it were only the amount on the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass.
One should not eat kodrava grain, nor should one sleep upon its straw.
Even that which is drunk would intoxicate; therefore, even that which is to be drunk is not [permissible] here.
6. The training rule on abstaining from high and grand beds:
A mendicant should sleep on a bed with legs eight finger-widths long according to the measure of the Victor;
it should be without spikes, or on a frame, but not one made of gold or silver.
A mendicant should provide a covering for a bed belonging to the Saṅgha;
for robes and woolen blankets, three, two, or one layer is prescribed respectively.
Having placed [the pillars] in the pits with a measurement not exceeding the thickness of their bases,
and having inserted them into each foot, one should mark them or fix them with stakes.
In this way, for the sake of protecting sugarcane, barley, and so forth, an ascetic should sleep on a bed;
while traveling on a long-footed road, he should not let his feet hang down.
If there are few [monks], then one dwelling-place (vihāraka) should indeed be assigned from among twelve;
if the number is very small, it should be with hands empty [of goods], but if the number is large, the opposite is the case. Śghs 3.6.5.
If there is little space, the junior monk may sleep on a seat and the elder on a couch;
even so, the junior must sleep at the foot of a tree or in the open air.
During the rains retreat, another fellow practitioner must not be assigned as an attendant; rather, within his own monastery, the ascetic should serve the ascetic according to seniority.
The bedding and seating belonging to the Saṅgha is designated for the sake of the enjoyment of conditioned things and for their preservation [for the ascetics].
Having established three types of dwellings— inferior, mediocre, and superior— for the monks,
one should assign them to the elders, newcomers, and others according to their seniority.
For a mendicant, a bed or seat that is too high is forbidden,
because it causes intoxication and restlessness, and is a cause for the world's reproach.
7. The training rule regarding the abstention from dancing, singing, and instrumental music:
one should not perform dancing with the flailing of arms, nor sing loudly, nor play musical instruments such as the lute, the flute, the drum, and so forth. Śghs_3,7.1 //
The training rule regarding the abstention from perfumes, garlands, and ointments:
a sick ascetic may wear sandalwood and other such fragrances after first giving them to the Sage at the word of a physician or similar authority. (Śghs 3.8.1)
One should not remain in a public place; having washed [the hands], one should go outside.
By this very procedure, one should wear a garland of flowers.
For one suffering from eye pain, headache, or affliction by the Pūtanā spirit,
one should wrap the head with a garland and not let the girdle hang down.
An ascetic should not, for the sake of color, apply yellow orpiment or other powders, or fragrant oils, to his face or any part of his body.
Because perfumes, garlands, and ointments are unbecoming for a renunciant,
and because they produce passion and agitation, they have been censured by the Victors.
One should not look at one's face in a mirror or in an oil vessel;
rather, it should be viewed by means of something else, for [looking otherwise] causes headache and illness.
One should not anoint one's own face with oil for the sake of adornment;
nor should one anoint it with anything else except in cases of cracked lips or diseases of the head.
An ascetic should not adorn his face with powders such as saffron;
however, for the purpose of healing a boil, an ointment made from sesame seeds and similar substances is permitted.
Regarding the training rule of abstaining from eating at improper times:
while I was eating at night, free from illness arose;
likewise indeed must it be done by you—you should eat only during the day. (Śghs 3.9.1)
People lamented, "They wander about our houses for the sake of their bellies, falling into pits of excrement and urine, and encountering thieves and snakes. (Śghs 3.9.2)
In the evening and in the morning, they wander for the sake of alms and likewise eat in assembly halls,
at crossroads, at junctions of three roads, in temples, and in houses.
The Sugata said: "A mendicant should eat at the proper time."
When the sun has risen and it is midday, at a time not exceeding the measure of a hair's breadth [of shadow].

Barley meal, boiled rice, and sour gruel; fish and meat that may be consumed at any time; and, for as long as one lives, [the use of] oil and so forth, with the exception of long pepper and fermented liquors.
Whatever is chewed with the teeth or swallowed down the throat,
one should eat that at the prescribed time so as not to cause distension of the belly.
A mendicant afflicted by thirst may eat flour and other such things free from meat, as well as mud-free water, hailstones, or ice.
When taking water for use, one should first wash both hands if they are stained with blood;
however, when washing the fingers, one should not take water that is already fit for use.
One who is possessed of deceit and guile should not perform their washing;
if those two [feet] are accompanied by sound, they are known to be pure for the ascetic whose skin is supple.
"If you do not give me food to eat, I shall die, tormented by hunger and thirst"—
if he speaks thus, he should be cast into a pit of hot embers.
If one should offer washed grain into a vessel that contains no meat,
it is clearly not permissible for a sick person to drink it.
One should avoid, like poisoned food, the dwellings, robes, and alms-food acquired through verbal and physical actions incited by greed.
One who observes the vow must not cause the sale of liquor, weapons, poison, living beings, or lac,
nor should he do so himself, nor should he make a livelihood by means of such things.
Indeed, hypocrisy for the sake of honor and gain is the restraint of the senses;
while flattery and sweet speech are practiced for the sake of obtaining clothing and other such things.
Solicitation is the disparagement of others for the sake of obtaining food and so forth;
it is also the conditional praise of another's bowl or other requisites.
The desire for gain through further gain, and the seeking of the increase of gains—
let the ascetic avoid these forms of wrong livelihood as he would excrement.
One who observes the vows should always avoid excessive playfulness, violence, and the excesses of body and speech, just as one avoids a snake smeared with dung.
In markets, in the vicinity of shrines and the like, as well as in gambling dens and houses of confinement, the *cellaka* shall not remain in those places which have been declared off-limits.
The training precept regarding abstaining from the acceptance of gold and silver:
the observer of the vow, with his body, hands, feet, robes, parasols, and so forth, should not touch silver or gold, as if they were a blazing fire. (Śghs 3.10.1)
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Means for Becoming a Śrāmaṇera," in the *Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha* compiled by Saṃghasena.
The Fourth Chapter: Other Customs; Campū, Kalaha, Dantāda, Kāṣṭha, Vṛddhāntika, and Yati.
One who is preoccupied with bathing, drinking, eating, and chanting, and who is naked or clad in a single garment.
Busying himself with work on clay, walking quickly even over two or three stories, hurrying along, cooking the bowl, and being distracted by work on his robes. (Śghs 4.2)

One who is intent on the preparation of powders and garments, one whose eyes are smeared with ointment, one who inhales smoke, or even one who writes or reads a book—such a person is not [a true practitioner]. Śghs 4.3.

A renunciant should not salute another renunciant who is going to a latrine or a place for urination, who is standing in the dark, who is pointing [with a finger], or who is putting on or covering his clothes. Śghs 4.4.
One should not place a footstool for the knees with one's head covered or wearing shoes,
just as one would never give a cracked skull to a person.
Seated in the samavasthā posture, while his two feet are being venerated, he should seize a crab and say, "May there be health! (Śghs 4.6).
This supplementary section on conduct has been extracted from the *Bhikṣuvinayasaṃkṣepa*;
it should be heard from one's preceptor and cultivated with reverence.
By the merit of this well-composed *Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha*, compiled by me in two hundred [verses], may all people attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "Other Conducts," in the *Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha* compiled by Saṃghasena.
Thus ends the *Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha*.
